plot_arc.inciting_incident: Recording underneath high-tension power wires resulting in massive electrical hum and an apparent audio-video clock desync, kicking off an adventure into AI forensics and articles on verifiable competence.
plot_arc.rising_action: Prompting frontier models for audio restoration and watching them produce authoritative, hallucinated DSP pipelines and bogus drift ratios, followed by returning to the trail to re-attempt the physical scenario under the conductors.
plot_arc.climax: Constructing deterministic Python DSP notch filters and spectral gating to salvage the audio, verifying whether the filter was a brittle one-off or a reproducible general-purpose tool.
plot_arc.resolution: The cautionary realization that when AI models project fluent competence far beyond our ability to verify, sovereign testing and empirical ground truth are the only real safeguards against catastrophic failure.

narrative.core_inquiry: When AI models project effortless confidence across specialized technical domains, how does an experienced engineer determine where competence ends and plausible falsehood begins?
narrative.chicago_context: Echoes the early Chicago craftsmanship ethos: rejecting vendor marketing claims in favor of empirical, reproducible tests and shared practitioner honesty.
narrative.ai_era_parallel: The defining challenge of Staff+ engineering in 2026: maintaining cognitive control over system boundaries rather than passively accepting synthetic code generation. Grounded in the Watts synthesis: Alan Watts warned IBM engineers in 1969 not to mistake the net of discrete tokens for the living organism, while Peter Watts demonstrated in Blindsight that high-throughput symbol manipulation can simulate intelligence without comprehension.

teleprompter_script.act_1:
[SCENE: Cam on desk]
In October 2026 I walked out under 345,000-volt transmission lines in Northern Illinois
with a smartphone to record some thoughts on software craftsmanship.
When I got back to my desk and checked the footage, the audio was destroyed.
60 Hz electromagnetic hum. Corona arcing. And what looked like a three-and-a-half-minute
clock drift between audio and video.
[FREEFORM: Describe what it felt like sitting there staring at the waveform - the instinct to just trash it and reshoot]
The standard advice is: trash it, reshoot.
Instead, I opened a browser tab and started asking AI models what to do.
That's how this series started.
[PAUSE]
This is The Sound Above: Minus Zero. I'm Mike Hall.
The bottleneck in engineering is never generation. It's verification.
teleprompter_script.act_2:
[SCENE: Terminal - show the original prompt or a browser tab with the chat]
I started with thirteen words in a browser. Then brought it into Gemini Flash via the terminal.
The model immediately went to work.
Cascaded Butterworth filters. Exact duration ratios. Shell scripts. DSP pipelines.
It told me with total, unblinking confidence that the audio had drifted by twenty percent.
atempo=0.837. Here's the command. Run it.
[SHOW: The actual bad atempo command the model produced]
And it was completely wrong.
[FREEFORM: Talk about the sticker on the 2009 Dell Studio XPS from the Obtiva days: "Typing is not the bottleneck."
Talk about what that meant then vs what it means now - generating code is not the bottleneck, domain understanding is]
In Hollywood, they yell "Enhance!" and pixels appear from nowhere.
In software, that wishful thinking produces AI slop.
[PAUSE: let that sit]
The bottleneck is domain understanding. Same as it was in 2009.
teleprompter_script.act_3:
[SCENE: Show waveform or terminal output]
The container said: 21 minutes of video. 18 minutes of audio.
The model assumed linear drift and handed me atempo=0.837.
[SHOW: Audio waveform slurred - before fix]
When I tested it in headphones, the speech was slurred and completely out of sync.
[FREEFORM: Talk about what going back to ground truth feels like - the discipline of not trusting the answer just because it came out confidently]
So we went back to ground truth.
High-FPS frame extraction. Whisper subtitle alignment. Audio waveforms.
What had actually happened?
At 18 minutes I said "Thank you" and wrapped the talk.
The remaining three and a half minutes was me walking in silence with the camera still running.
The speech was at 1.0x the whole time.
[PAUSE]
When AI models project effortless competence, how do you find the boundary?
You verify with empirical tests. Not conversational trust.
teleprompter_script.act_4:
[SCENE: Show phone diagram or dual-mic diagram slide]
[SHOW: Diagram of iPhone dual-mic placement - top mic vs bottom mic]
Here's what was actually going on with the audio.
Modern smartphones use dual mics for noise suppression.
The mic at the top was acting as an unshielded inductive loop antenna.
Picking up 65 times more electromagnetic interference from the overhead towers
than the bottom mic.
[SHOW: Spectral waterfall - before and after isolating bottom mic]
Isolating the bottom mic gave us clean speech buried under the noise.
[FREEFORM: Talk about the decision to go back out under those same wires.
What you wanted to prove - was the dehum filter a one-time lucky fix or a real tool?]
And I didn't leave it there as a single lucky fix.
I walked back out under those same 345kV conductors.
Deliberately re-attempted the scenario. Same trail, same conductors.
I wanted to know: is this filter real, or was it one good day?
[SHOW: Second field recording footage if cued, or just the trail photo]
teleprompter_script.act_5:
[SCENE: Terminal - show the deterministic filter running]
[DEMO: Run the dehum filter against the second field recording - show timing output]
That field re-test gets to the heart of the cautionary tale.
When you prompt a frontier model outside your domain, it hands you math and code
with total, fluent confidence. You look like an audio engineering expert.
But you're throwing a ball high into the air.
If you throw it too high, far beyond what you can verify and catch,
it comes straight down on your head.
[SHOW: just3ws.localhost/dehum/dashboard.html - the A/B listening comparison]
[FREEFORM: Walk through what the dashboard shows - the raw audio, the hum-removed audio,
the spectral diff, the filter parameters that survived the second test]
When we ran the re-attempt footage through the same pipeline, the parameters held.
40 milliseconds. Stripped the hum. Preserved clean voice.
But the warning stands: AI models simulate mastery without comprehension.
Like the Chinese room in Peter Watts' Blindsight.
Our job isn't to marvel at synthetic fluency.
Our job is to walk back under the wires and test the boundary.

[FREEFORM: Talk about what that moment felt like - the realization that the thing you'd been waiting a decade for was now just... free]
But I didn't want to risk the UGtastic tapes on unverified tools.
I needed a massive, clean dataset first. Something I could break things on.
I needed a single consistent speaker. Hundreds of hours. No crosstalk. No panel noise.
[PAUSE]
That's how I found Dead Rabbit Radio.
[SHOW: deadrabbitradio.com in browser]
teleprompter_script.act_4:
[SCENE: Show the fluffle GitHub repo in browser or terminal]
[SHOW: github.com/just3ws/fluffle]
Dead Rabbit Radio. Jason Carpenter. Daily paranormal folklore. Solo host.
Zero crosstalk, no mic swaps, consistent cadence.
And honestly? His speaking rhythm is a lot like mine.
I had five Raspberry Pi boards in my home lab. node01 through node05.
[FREEFORM: Describe the physical setup - where the Pis sat, what the basement looked like, how janky the whole rig was]
I wrote bin/distribution in Ruby to bin-pack the audio files across nodes by byte size.
bin/distribute pushed files via Net::SSH and rsync.
On each Pi, bin/transcribe ran whisper.cpp with a mandatory 120-second thermal cooldown between jobs.
[SHOW: The actual bin/transcribe script open in terminal or editor]
No heatsinks. Just stock boards. Sixty seconds of compute, two minutes of cooling. Repeat.
teleprompter_script.act_5:
[SCENE: Back on cam]
For several weeks that cluster just hummed in my basement.
It generated 2,034 distinct transcript files.
Text, subtitles. Over a thousand episodes.
I reached out to Jason on Discord to ask his blessing.
[FREEFORM: Talk about that conversation - how it felt to reach out, what Jason said, why it mattered to get that blessing before shipping anything]
He was genuinely gracious. Kind. Supportive. More than I expected.
And then I hit the cliff.
[PAUSE: this is the hard part, let it land]
I tried to turn fluffle into a universal podcast aggregator.
Immediately: broken RSS feeds. Corrupted ID3 tags. Erratic audio formats everywhere.
At the same time, high-severity production incidents at the day job.
Observability architecture work that was consuming everything I had.
[FREEFORM: Talk about what working memory exhaustion actually feels like - not as a clinical term, but as a lived thing. The tab-switching. The feeling of losing the thread.]
I told myself I was an imposter playing with toy scripts.
I froze. Stopped committing. Stopped responding to Jason on Discord.
For months I couldn't even bring myself to open the repo or listen to the show.
teleprompter_script.act_6:
[SCENE: Show the running pipeline dashboard or ztranscribe output in terminal]
For a long time I carried fluffle as a private regret.
[FREEFORM: Talk about what changed - when you picked it back up, what you were able to see from a distance that you couldn't see up close]
But craftsmanship teaches you to inspect your scars honestly.
That experiment wasn't a failure. It was the essential skunkworks lab that made today possible.
It taught me: normalize audio deterministically before running inference.
It taught me Maildir queue architecture. It taught me lexical priming for proper nouns.
And it proved local hardware sovereignty works.
[SHOW: ztranscribe running on a UGtastic interview file, timing output visible]
Five Raspberry Pis taking two hours per episode.
Now it's Apple Silicon. Ninety seconds. All 218 UGtastic interviews: transcribed and searchable.
[PAUSE]
To Jason Carpenter: thank you. For the stories, the generosity, and the craft.
The sticker stays on the laptop.
The lessons are in every line of code this system runs today.
[SCENE: Outro card / Patreon link]
If you want to support the archive and the independent hosting behind it:
patreon.com/whoistechcmty
Next up: Episode Zero. Minus Zero. The Mirage of Competence.
Keep your feedback loops fast.

narrative.tone: Reflective, technical, practitioner-focused, and direct
narrative.topic: Phalanx Duel: Make the Rules Legible

plot_arc.inciting_incident: A rainy week at Boy Scout Camp Tesomas in July 2022 leads to designing a 1v1 tactical card duel on standard 52-card playing cards with zero dice and no mid-game shuffle.
plot_arc.rising_action: Prototyping combat rules in Ruby, translating tabletop formations into a deterministic, server-authoritative TypeScript engine, and releasing a Go CLI client.
plot_arc.climax: Presenting the architecture at Software Craftsmanship McHenry County, demonstrating how replay fingerprints, role-safe projections, and action ledgers establish unambiguous ground truth.
plot_arc.resolution: Proving that in an era of non-deterministic AI generation, legible rules and verifiable state boundaries are the foundation of trustworthy production systems.

narrative.core_inquiry: How do you build a system where the physical rules at a table, the network protocol, client projections, and operational ledgers all agree about what happened?
narrative.chicago_context: Grounded in the McHenry County and Chicago software craftsmanship tradition of empirical testing, boundary visibility, and learning through deliberate, reproducible practice.
narrative.ai_era_parallel: LLMs and generative agents cannot be trusted with hidden state or rules authority; they require bounded MCP interfaces, deterministic simulation engines, and cryptographic verification.

teleprompter_script.act_1:
[SCENE: Cam on desk, cards visible if possible]
July 2022. Rainy week at Boy Scout Camp Tesomas, northern Wisconsin.
Wooden picnic table. Two standard 52-card decks. A notebook.
[FREEFORM: Set the scene physically - the rain on the pavilion roof, the mud, the scouts around you,
why you were thinking about card game design instead of whatever you were supposed to be doing]
I wanted to design a two-player tactical duel with zero dice and no mid-match shuffles.
Every outcome had to come strictly from the cards on the table
and the deliberate choices each player made.
That became Phalanx Duel.
[SHOW: The two-page quickstart PDF or the phalanxduel.com landing page]
This is The Sound Above: Special Presentation. I'm Mike Hall.
Today we're talking about cards, state machines, and why making rules legible
is the deepest responsibility of software craftsmanship.
teleprompter_script.act_2:
[SCENE: Terminal open with Ruby script]
[DEMO: Show the Ruby combat prototype running - suit interactions, column defense math, damage propagation]
[SHOW: github.com/phalanxduel or the specific bin/ scripts in the repo]
To prove the rules worked, I started where craftsmen start: executable code.
In Phalanx Duel, each player controls an eight-card formation.
Two ranks across four columns.
When an attack hits a column, damage chews through the front-rank vanguard first,
then the rear-rank flank, before it can reach Life Points.
[FREEFORM: Walk through a sample combat turn in the terminal. Explain what the Ruby output means.
Show the suit interaction rules. Point out where edge cases showed up during early testing
and what that told you about the rules design.]
The rules were simple enough for two scouts on a soggy bench.
Precise enough to run identically in software.
A working prototype is only the beginning.
teleprompter_script.act_3:
[SCENE: Show WebSocket diagram or TypeScript server code]
[DEMO: Show the TypeScript engine structure - the intent handler, the state machine, the action ledger]
The real challenge was turning tabletop rules into a live multiplayer architecture.
Many game architectures make the mistake of trusting the client to resolve moves.
In Phalanx Duel, the client never dictates state.
It sends player intent over a WebSocket connection.
The server validates that intent against current deterministic state,
computes the next transition,
and records the exact action in an immutable ledger.
[FREEFORM: Talk about why client-authority is the wrong model for anything where integrity matters.
Connect it to the same problem in production systems: hidden state, unverifiable transitions,
no ground truth for what actually happened.]
What a table verifies with physical cards is what the server enforces on every turn.
The boundary is the same. The discipline is the same.
teleprompter_script.act_4:
[SCENE: Show role-safe projection diagram or the network protocol flow]
[SHOW: Slide or diagram - what Player 1 sees vs Player 2 sees vs Spectator sees]
Determinism is necessary but not sufficient.
An engine can be 100 percent deterministic while executing completely flawed logic.
To bridge that gap: replay fingerprints, action verification hashes, role-safe projections.
The authoritative server maintains complete match state, including facedown cards.
When broadcasting updates, it projects only what each role should see.
Player 1 gets their private hand. Player 2 gets theirs.
Spectators get a time-delayed broadcast.
[FREEFORM: Connect role-safe projections to information security in distributed production systems.
Talk about where you've seen the same problem in enterprise contexts: services that broadcast too much,
or clients that trust themselves to compute state they don't own.]
The protocol itself becomes an active guardian of the game's integrity.
teleprompter_script.act_5:
[SCENE: Back on cam or show SCMC slides]
[FREEFORM: This act should be mostly improvised. Here are the anchors:]
In September 2026 I brought this to Software Craftsmanship McHenry County.
The talk: Make the Rules Legible.
[FREEFORM: Talk honestly about the experiment of building the whole presentation with AI tooling.
What accelerated. What completely fell apart. What the model got confidently wrong about your own talk.
The meta-lesson from using AI to build a presentation about AI's limits.
Don't script this - just tell it as it happened.]
The meta-lesson: generative tools accelerate scaffolding dramatically.
But without human stewardship and deterministic boundaries, they hallucinate fluently.
The model can suggest moves. Only an authoritative engine can verify the truth.
[PAUSE: let the irony land]
teleprompter_script.act_6:
[SCENE: Browser - phalanxduel.com ranked ladder]
[SHOW: phalanxduel.com - the live ranked ladder, current match count if visible]
Phalanx Duel is live in production today.
Automated release pipelines. Containerized deployments. Glicko-2 ranked ladder.
[SHOW: YouTube playlist - youtube.com/playlist?list=PLHenvAZhJjHo]
[FREEFORM: Talk about Conrad Hall's walkthrough video - 15 years old, high school sophomore,
AP Computer Science, co-developer. What it means to watch a kid that age pick up
rules-as-code and run with it. Keep it brief, keep it genuine.]
Download the rules, inspect the engine, play a match: phalanxduel.com
The lessons from that Wisconsin picnic table:
server authority, deterministic replay, visible boundaries, zero-indirection state transitions.
Those are the same disciplines we're here to talk about across The Sound Above.
Keep your rules legible. Keep your boundaries explicit.
Keep your systems safe to change.
